name: frege
desc: Non-strict, functional programming language in the spirit of Haskell
why: A Haskell-inspired language running on the JVM; uncommon and worth a curious afternoon.

brief.what_it_is: Frege is a purely functional, non-strict (lazy) programming language described by its author as a Haskell for the JVM. It compiles Frege source to Java (the README says it produces a .class and a .java file per module) and runs on the Java Virtual Machine. Frege code can call any Java library, and Java code can call Frege functions. The compiler is the fregec executable. The README says most vanilla Haskell code runs unmodified or with minor changes, and that the standard library supports almost all of Haskell 2010.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents Frege as a way for Java programmers to learn a pure functional paradigm and for Haskell programmers to use their skills on the JVM, while keeping access to Java's libraries. It says Frege keeps Haskell's guarantees, such as purity, thread safety and lazy evaluation, even when it calls Java code.
brief.how_it_works: Functions are checked by a strong static type system with global type inference, so purity is carried in the types. Pure functions are described as stateless and safe to cache automatically, and the README suggests the compiler could use this for optimizations such as precalculation, deferred execution and common subexpression elimination. Main is typed IO (), and the type system requires any caller of an IO function to also be IO, so impurity propagates up the call chain. Calling Java from Frege requires declaring the Java types in Frege terms.
brief.install_notes: The README requires at least JDK 7 to compile and run programs. The compiler, an Eclipse plugin and provisional documentation are downloaded from the GitHub releases page. Getting started at the command line is covered on the project wiki's Getting Started page, which I did not fetch. Build tool support is listed for Maven, Gradle, Leiningen, SBT and Bazel. Editor support includes the Eclipse plugin, a VS Code plugin and an IntelliJ IDEA plugin that is still under development. The README also points to an online REPL at try.fregelang.org, so you can try it without installing anything.
brief.standout: Purity is encoded in the type system, and the README uses a Hello World with a pure greeting function and an IO main to show the idea of islands of purity in a sea of imperative code. Most of the compiler, standard library, REPL and documentation tool are written in Frege itself, which the README offers as evidence of stability.
brief.status: unknown. The README gives no release version or date, and I did not check the releases or commit history. The copyright line says 2011-2022. The README also links a Travis CI badge at travis-ci.org and a Freenode IRC channel, both of which may be out of date. The project appears to have been active through about 2022 and to be quiet since, but I could not confirm this from the page.
brief.caveats: The README says the documentation is provisional. Some Haskell differences remain, listed on a wiki page I did not fetch. The Hoogle instance for Frege is disabled due to domain issues. The IntelliJ plugin is still under development. The README says Frege requires JDK 7 or later. Code that uses JVM-specific features will not run on other Haskell compilers.
quotes: Frege is a Haskell for the JVM.
Frege compiles to Java, runs on the JVM, and uses any Java library you want.
Most idiomatic Haskell code will run in Frege unmodified or with only minimal, obvious adaptations.
Frege is named after and in honor of Gottlob Frege who published the ideas of higher-order functions, partial function application, and many more concepts of formal logic
